 An opportunity to rethink flood resilience for Bangkok
 Thailand’s proposed THB165 billion (US$4.91 billion) flood diversion project presents an opportunity to rethink flood management – combining engineering with natural floodplains, wetlands and river restoration to strengthen long-term resilience.
 As Thailand plans major flood protection investments, experts are calling for a broader approach that restores natural river systems – reducing long-term costs while safeguarding biodiversity, livelihoods and downstream communities. Image:  Philip Roeland , CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Flickr .
 https://eb.news/CxVnzvRnTkyA 
 Copy 
 By 
 Sang Lee and 
 Marc Goichot 
 5 minute read
 Nov. 11, 2026 
 For families and businesses affected by Thailand’s floods, the immediate priority is clear: safety, recovery and confidence that the next monsoon will bring less hardship. The government’s willingness to invest in flood protection is welcome. The question now is how to ensure that investment delivers the greatest lasting benefit for people and nature 
 The recently announced THB165 billion (US$4.91 billion) flood diversion project offers an opportunity to look beyond a single structure and consider the future of the whole basin. Could Thailand use this moment to bring its best expertise and its communities together around a broader ambition: making the Chao Phraya a stronger partner in resilience? 
 There is good reason to ask. It is also a timely question as Bangkok Climate Week brings together policymakers, businesses, researchers and civil society to discuss climate resilience and sustainable development. 
 This river and its seasonal floods helped create the plains and delta on which Bangkok, much of Thailand’s food production and a rich cultural heritage depend. The challenge is to retain those life-giving functions while reducing the danger to people. Protecting Bangkok also means protecting the processes that built its foundations. 
 “
 Natural systems have a capacity for self-renewal: vegetation regrows, seasonal flows replenish wetlands, and sediment rebuilds land where conditions allow. With space and good stewardship, those processes can reduce reliance on repeated dredging, pumping and structural repairs. 
 Other countries are rethinking this relationship. The Netherlands’ Room for the River programme, floodplain restoration in Germany and efforts to restore space for rivers in France reflect a wider European shift. 
 In the United States, the Army Corps of Engineers’ Engineering With Nature initiative also brings natural processes into engineering design. These approaches draw on experience of the limits and costs of relying too heavily on confinement and control. 
 Thailand has the chance to apply those lessons now, adapting them to its own landscape and knowledge. A government-led, inclusive comparison of options would demonstrate foresight and strengthen public confidence in whatever investments follow. 
 Nature is infrastructure 
 Extreme rainfall is part of the challenge, but so is the condition of the land receiving it. Changes in catchments, roads and drainage can concentrate runoff faster, while floodplain development removes places where water once spread and slowed. Climate change makes recovering that lost resilience more urgent. 
 Healthy catchments can slow runoff. Wetlands and connected floodplains act as natural reservoirs, reducing flood peaks where storage is available at the right time and place. Bangkok’s Benjakitti Forest Park already illustrates the value of natural stormwater storage. There is scope to explore that principle across the basin. 
 Water is only half the river’s story. Flowing water and sediment together shape the depth, width and bends of its channels. Floods carry sediment onto floodplains, replenishing soils and building land. Sediment reaching the coast helps sustain the delta. These connections explain why a change in one place can have consequences many kilometres away. 
 Dams and reservoirs illustrate the trade-off. They can buffer flood peaks, but also trap sediment needed downstream. Reduced sediment supply can alter channels and deprive floodplains and coasts of material that helps maintain land elevation and counter erosion. 
 By sustaining coastal land and wetlands, sediment also supports natural protection against waves and storm-surge impacts. Benefits during one flood season therefore need to be considered alongside effects elsewhere in the basin over decades. 
 This is also an economic question. Natural systems have a capacity for self-renewal: vegetation regrows, seasonal flows replenish wetlands, and sediment rebuilds land where conditions allow. With space and good stewardship, those processes can reduce reliance on repeated dredging, pumping and structural repairs. Continually resisting them can make construction only the first instalment of a much longer bill. 
 Working with such powerful processes is a practical investment strategy. Connected floodplains can provide storage while sustaining fisheries, farming and wildlife. Keeping sediment and sand within the functioning river system can contribute to climate resilience. The potential savings and benefits deserve the same serious assessment as any major engineering proposal. 
 For the delta, that assessment must include land renewal. Limiting groundwater extraction is necessary but cannot remove natural compaction or by itself ensure that land keeps pace with rising seas. Research and action on sediment delivery and deposition can help complete the picture: where is new land being built, where is replenishment interrupted, and what could restore it? 
 A shared decision for the next generation 
 Thailand has deep experience of living with seasonal water. Combining that knowledge with modern forecasting, safer buildings and adapted farming could open possibilities that a drainage-only discussion misses. Communities offering space for floodwater should help design the arrangements and share fairly in the benefits, including compensation where needed. 
 The gains extend to food and culture. Tropical rivers support extraordinary fish diversity, much of it threatened. WWF’s Living Planet Report 2024 documented an average 85 per cent decline in monitored freshwater wildlife populations since 1970. 
 Healthy fisheries underpin affordable protein, livelihoods, local markets, Thai cuisine and tourism. The Forgotten Fishes reports and the Emergency Recovery Plan for freshwater biodiversity reinforce the importance of restoring habitats, flows and connectivity. 
 The government could convene an assessment bringing engineers and disaster-risk specialists together with experts in sediment and river processes, ecologists, economists, planners, businesses and local communities. This would give technical expertise a wider foundation and help build agreement on the choices ahead. 
 The task would be clear: compare the proposed works with natural storage and different combinations of nature and engineering. Assess protection under future climate conditions, costs over the full operating life, and risks transferred to other communities. Include benefits to food production, biodiversity and land renewal. Publish the evidence and explain the trade-offs before long-term commitments narrow the options. 
 This could turn a major flood investment into a transition from DDD—drain, dam and dike—towards CCC: connectivity along rivers, connectivity between rivers and floodplains, and connectivity between surface water and groundwater. In everyday terms, that means keeping routes open for water, sediment and fish, giving floods safe places to spread, and sustaining the exchanges that support wetlands and aquifers. Targeted engineering would help make that system work safely for people. 
 There is an opportunity here for leaders in Bangkok and across Thailand to demonstrate a kind of stewardship whose value grows over time: bringing people together, testing alternatives openly and leaving room to adapt. Future generations will inherit both the protection we build and the costs we commit them to. They deserve decisions informed by the full range of options available today. 
 The Chao Phraya helped build Thailand. Making its processes our partners could be one of the most valuable legacies of this investment.
